newsitem.title: UK: Britain says up to IRA to break peace logjam.
newsitem.headline: Britain says up to IRA to break peace logjam.

text.p: Britain, struggling to revive the flagging Northern Ireland peace process, on Sunday urged the Irish Republican Army (IRA) to call a lasting ceasefire and told the guerrilla group the "the ball is now in your court."

"They must demonstrate openly and convincingly that this time their ceasefire would be for real and would be for good," Northern Ireland Minister Michael Ancram said after the latest peace feelers from Sinn Fein, the IRA's political wing.
Protestant Unionists, who want to maintain Northern Ireland's links with Britain, echoed the government line and said they saw little sign of an imminent ceasefire.

Sinn Fein held a one-day party "conflict resolution" conference on Saturday in a climate of uncertainty about a peace process that suffered a severe setback in February when the IRA, which is battling to oust Britain from Northern Ireland, set off bombs in London.

Party strategist Martin McGuinness said after the conference in the Irish Republic that Britain had been given proposals from moderate nationalist leader John Hume and Sinn Fein leader Gerry Adams more than a month ago but had not yet responded.
Adams said: "What we need now is the courage from (British Prime Minister John) Major. The key is in his hands."
Ancram responded after the Sinn Fein meeting with a statement that showed there was little sign of any progress.

"The PIRA (Provisional IRA) ceasefire should be restored immediately. It should never have been ended. As the sole perpetrators of the violence they alone can restore the ceasefire. The ball is firmly in PIRA's court," he said.

"If they do so in a way which is genuinely unequivocal, that is to say in a way which is both credible and dependable, then they can end the self-imposed exclusion of Sinn Fein from the talks process and from democratic dialogue on the future of Northern Ireland," he added.

On prospects of a ceasefire, Ulster Unionisty Party leader David Trimble said: "We see no sign of it. The advice that we hear from the police and the security services is that there is no sign of a commitment to peace.
"The current talk of peace is merely camouflage behind which their preparations for violence advance," he told BBC Television.
"The last ceasefire was not genuine, even at its very outset....There is no reason why we should be taken in again.
